title: Billboard Hot 100 Number Ones
text:
For this analysis, I used the Billboard Hot 100 Number Ones dataset featured in TidyTuesday.
The dataset contains information about songs that reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 between 1958 and January 2025. It includes information about the songs’ artists, genres, length, musical characteristics, and chart performance.
The original dataset was compiled by Chris Dalla Riva as part of his Billboard Hot 100 Number Ones Database.

text:
For this analysis, I used the Billboard Hot 100 Number Ones dataset featured in TidyTuesday.
The dataset contains information about songs that reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 between 1958 and January 2025. It includes information about the songs’ artists, genres, length, musical characteristics, and chart performance.

title: Billboard Hot 100 Number Ones
text:
Load the Data


Code
library(tidyverse)

billboard <- readr::read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-08-26/billboard.csv"
)

topics <- readr::read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-08-26/topics.csv"
)

title: Billboard Hot 100 Number Ones
text:
Have Number-One Songs Gotten Shorter?
One question I was interested in was whether the length of number-one songs has changed over time. The dataset includes length_sec, which measures the length of each song in seconds. I converted this to minutes to make the visualization easier to interpret.


Code
billboard_length <- billboard |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(format(date, "%Y")),
    length_min = length_sec / 60
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(length_min))

ggplot(
  billboard_length,
  aes(x = year, y = length_min)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess") +
  labs(
    title = "Length of Billboard Hot 100 Number-One Songs Over Time",
    subtitle = "Each point represents a song that reached number one",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Song length (minutes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









The trend line makes it easier to see how the typical length of a number-one song has changed over time. Song lengths increased during parts of the late 20th century, but more recent number-one hits appear to have become shorter.

title: Billboard Hot 100 Number Ones
section: Which Genres Have the Most Number-One Hits?
text:
Which Genres Have the Most Number-One Hits?
I also wanted to see which genres appear most frequently among number-one songs. The variable cdr_genre gives the genre assigned to each song in the dataset.


Code
top_genres <- billboard |>
  filter(!is.na(cdr_genre)) |>
  count(cdr_genre, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

ggplot(
  top_genres,
  aes(
    x = reorder(cdr_genre, n),
    y = n
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Genres With the Most Billboard Hot 100 Number-One Songs",
    x = "Genre",
    y = "Number of number-one songs"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









This visualization shows which genres have accounted for the largest number of Billboard Hot 100 number-one songs in the dataset.

title: NCAA Men’s March Madness
text:
For this analysis, I used the NCAA Men’s March Madness dataset featured in TidyTuesday.
The data come from Nishaan Amin’s March Madness dataset and contain historical team tournament results along with public predictions for tournament teams.
The data cover men’s NCAA tournaments from 2008 through 2024, excluding 2020 because the tournament was canceled.

title: NCAA Men’s March Madness
text:
For this analysis, I used the NCAA Men’s March Madness dataset featured in TidyTuesday.
The data come from Nishaan Amin’s March Madness dataset and contain historical team tournament results along with public predictions for tournament teams.
The data cover men’s NCAA tournaments from 2008 through 2024, excluding 2020 because the tournament was canceled.

title: NCAA Men’s March Madness
text:
Load the Data


Code
library(tidyverse)

team_results <- readr::read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-03-26/team-results.csv"
)

public_picks <- readr::read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-03-26/public-picks.csv"
)

title: NCAA Men’s March Madness
section: Which Teams Have Made the Most Final Fours?
text:
Which Teams Have Made the Most Final Fours?
The F4 variable gives the number of times each program reached the Final Four. I looked at the teams with the most Final Four appearances in the dataset.


Code
top_final_four <- team_results |>
  filter(F4 > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(F4)) |>
  slice_head(n = 15)

ggplot(
  top_final_four,
  aes(
    x = reorder(TEAM, F4),
    y = F4
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Teams With the Most Final Four Appearances",
    subtitle = "NCAA men's tournament results in the TidyTuesday dataset",
    x = "Team",
    y = "Final Four appearances"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









This visualization shows which programs have reached the Final Four most often over the period represented in the dataset.

title: NCAA Men’s March Madness
section: Which Teams Did the Public Most Expect to Win?
text:
Which Teams Did the Public Most Expect to Win?
The public_picks dataset contains the percentage of people who selected each team to advance through each round. The FINALS variable represents the percentage of public brackets picking a team to win in the championship round.
For each year, I identified the team with the highest public championship pick percentage.


Code
public_champion_picks <- public_picks |>
  mutate(
    finals_pct = readr::parse_number(FINALS)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(finals_pct)) |>
  group_by(YEAR) |>
  slice_max(
    order_by = finals_pct,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  ungroup()




Code
ggplot(
  public_champion_picks,
  aes(
    x = factor(YEAR),
    y = finals_pct
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = TEAM),
    hjust = -0.1,
    size = 3
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "The Public's Most Popular Championship Pick by Year",
    subtitle = "Team with the highest percentage of public picks to win the final",
    x = "Tournament year",
    y = "Public championship pick percentage"
  ) +
  expand_limits(y = max(public_champion_picks$finals_pct) + 10) +
  theme_minimal()









This plot shows how strongly the public favored its most popular championship pick in each tournament year. Some years had a clear favorite, while in other years public expectations were more spread out.

title: NCAA Men’s March Madness
section: Which Teams Did the Public Most Expect to Win in 2024?
text:
Which Teams Did the Public Most Expect to Win in 2024?
The public_picks dataset contains the percentage of public brackets that picked each team to advance through each round of the 2024 tournament. The FINALS variable gives the percentage of people who picked each team to win the championship.
I looked at the 10 teams with the highest championship pick percentages.


Code
top_public_picks <- public_picks |>
  mutate(
    finals_pct = readr::parse_number(FINALS)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(finals_pct)) |>
  arrange(desc(finals_pct)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

ggplot(
  top_public_picks,
  aes(
    x = reorder(TEAM, finals_pct),
    y = finals_pct
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Most Popular Public Picks to Win the 2024 Championship",
    subtitle = "Top 10 teams by percentage of public brackets",
    x = "Team",
    y = "Percent of public brackets picking team to win"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









Connecticut was the most popular public choice to win the championship in 2024, while several other highly rated teams also received substantial support. This visualization shows how concentrated public expectations were among the top contenders.
As a side note, UCONN went on to have one of the most dominant title runs in March Madness history, winning by a record average margin of 23 points per game.
